Hobson was born in Derby, the son of William Hobson, "a rather prosperous newspaper proprietor", and Josephine Atkinson.
He was the brother of the mathematician Ernest William Hobson.
He studied at Derby School and Lincoln College, Oxford and, after his graduation, taught classics and English literature at schools in Faversham and Exeter.
Early career
When Hobson relocated to London in 1887, England was in the midst of a major economic depression.
While classical economics was at a loss to explain the vicious business cycles, London had many societies that proposed alternatives.
While living in London, Hobson was exposed to the Social Democrats and H.M.
Hyndman, Christian Socialists, and Henry George's Single-tax system.
He befriended several of the prominent Fabians who would found the London School of Economics, some of whom he had known at Oxford.
During the very late 19th century, his works included Problems of Poverty, Evolution of Modern Capitalism, Problem of the Unemployed and John Ruskin: Social Reformer.
Boer War and imperialism
During his coverage of the Second Boer War, Hobson began to form the idea that imperialism was the direct result of the expanding forces of modern capitalism.
He believed the mine owners, led by Cecil Rhodes, wanted control of the Transvaal.

In a 1902 Political Science Quarterly article, Hobson challenged numerous moral justifications for imperialism, including the notion that "less efficient" races benefitted from subordination to "more efficient" races.
First World War and later career
Hobson's opposition to the First World War caused him to join the Union of Democratic Control.
His advocacy for the formation of a world political body to prevent wars can be found in his piece Towards International Government.
However, he became staunchly opposed to the League of Nations.
In 1919, Hobson joined the Independent Labour Party.
Hobson's autobiography Confessions of an Economic Heretic was published in 1938.

In Imperialism he advocated their "gradual elimination" by an international organization: "A rational stirpiculture in the wide social interest might, however, require a repression of the spread of degenerate or unprogressive races".
Antisemitism
Hobson's early works were critical of the impact of Jewish immigration and Jewish financiers.
In the 1890s he argued that large scale Jewish immigration from the Russian Partition to Western Europe harmed the interests of native workers and advocated limitations on immigration.
Writing on the South African war in War in South Africa, he linked the impetus towards war to "Jew Power" in South Africa and saw Johannesburg as a "New Jerusalem".
Hobson wrote that "Jewish financiers", whom he saw as "parasites", manipulated the British government that danced to their "diabolical tune".
According to history professor Norman Etherington, the section on financiers in Imperialism seems irrelevant to Hobson's economic discourse, and was probably included since Hobson truly believed it.

Jacob Little was born in Newburyport, Massachusetts on March 17, 1794.
The son of a successful local shipbuilder and of Quaker origin, Little exhibited a strong understanding of money and financial markets from an early age.

In 1817 he emigrated to New York City and became a clerk in the store of Jacob Barker, a highly successful financier, merchant, and politically well-connected founding member of the Democratic Party political machine Tammany Hall.
Little spent five years in apprenticeship under Barker before moving out in 1822 to start his own business with $700 he had accrued over the length of his employment.
Market operations
Although theoretically he could have asked for more, Little chose not to force the issue because he feared the resulting bankruptcies would destabilize the market potentially cause a collapse.
Approximately 60,000 shares had been sold short by that time, but only 7,000 shares had yet been issued; needless to say, Little prospered immensely.
After some troubles, Little was again worth $2 million by 1846.
The Panic of 1857 completely blindsided the investor, who at the time was "long", possessing huge amounts of stock, much bought on the "margin".
Later life and legacy
A speculator to his very core, Little never put away any of his fortune to prepare for a rainy day; any money he made on the stock market, he immediately invested back into it.
Thus when the Panic of 1857 destroyed his investment fortune, Little was left penniless.
He would live out the rest of his life under the wing of his last protége, David Groesbeck.
Little was only ever able to make small trading returns to the market in his later years, and the magnitude of his fall was often the target of mockery from his former peers.
Little died on March 28, 1865, and his funeral was held on March 31 at New York's Grace Church.

Nonetheless for all of his wealth and innovation Little's ignominious end ensured he was quickly forgotten, and by the time Edwin Lefèvre published his now-classic Reminiscences of a Stock Operator in 1923 he was virtually unknown.

He became Chief Accountant in 1955 and held a series of appointments in Hong Kong and Singapore, before becoming Chief Manager in 1962, succeeding Sir Michael Turner.
The board of directors of the bank up to this point was entirely non-executive but in 1962, exceptionally, he was elected to the board.
